title: Long-horizon work · Choosing an agent
description: Break extended work into resumable experiments with explicit state, gates and evidence. Match autonomy, cost and review effort to task risk, uncertainty and reversibility.

sections.title: Long-horizon work: accumulate evidence, not elapsed time

blocks.body:
The agent has been busy for two hours. It has read dozens of files, tried several patches and produced a long status report. What do we know now that we did not know at the start?

If that question is difficult to answer, more runtime may just buy more activity. Long tasks need intermediate results that can be checked and carried forward, especially when the work changes direction or moves to a fresh session.

blocks.title: A migration task may run across several sessions.
blocks.problem: A migration task may run across several sessions.

steps.title: Divide the route
steps.body: Stage one maps callers, stage two adds compatibility, stage three migrates one path, and stage four removes the old path only after evidence.
steps.reason: Each stage has a smaller proof and a safe stopping point.
steps.trap: Giving one prompt permission to rewrite every caller and delete the old API.

steps.title: Resume from state
steps.body: After each stage, record the revision, tests, unresolved questions and next gate.
steps.reason: A fresh run can continue without replaying the whole investigation.
steps.trap: Relying on the transcript as the only memory.

blocks.title: Make progress legible
blocks.body:
For a retry repair, the first stage might end with a deterministic reproduction, not a patch. The second ends with a candidate change and evidence that the reproduction now passes. The third checks surrounding behaviour and prepares the result for review.

These stages need not take equal time. Their value is that each answers a different question: can we reproduce it, does the change address it, and what else might the change affect?

After each stage, keep a short record of the revision, commands, findings and unresolved questions. If reproduction proves impossible without production access, stop there and report the missing evidence. Do not quietly replace the task with a plausible-looking cleanup.

blocks.bridge: Elapsed time is not evidence of progress.
blocks.meaning: A long task needs observable stage outcomes and resumable state.
blocks.question: An agent has edited twenty files but cannot say which hypothesis the changes test. What is missing?
blocks.answer: A progress contract: the task was not broken into stages with a decision, evidence and stopping condition.

further.question: What should a stage record?
further.answer: The goal, changed artifacts, observations, uncertainty and the next permitted experiment.

further.question: Why record rejected paths?
further.answer: They stop a resumed run from repeating work that already failed to explain the problem.

blocks.title: Use gates, not hope
blocks.body: Pause before expensive, risky or irreversible transitions. A gate can ask whether the hypothesis still fits, whether the tests are trustworthy and whether the next action remains inside scope. Long-horizon autonomy should be a sequence of bounded commitments, not one large permission slip.

blocks.bridge: Long-horizon work needs moments where autonomy narrows before risk rises.
blocks.meaning: Gates preserve human control at transitions where the next action changes cost, scope or reversibility.
blocks.question: When should a human approval gate appear?
blocks.answer: Before a consequential transition such as publishing, changing production configuration or committing to a broad refactor.

further.question: What makes a gate useful?
further.answer: It has a clear question and evidence to inspect, rather than asking for a vague feeling of confidence.

further.question: Should every small action need approval?
further.answer: No. Excessive gates destroy the benefit of delegation; use them where risk or irreversibility changes.

blocks.body: Long-horizon work is a chain of bounded experiments, each leaving enough evidence for the next one.
blocks.nextConnection: The final lesson in this unit asks the harder question: given the task, environment and horizon, how much autonomy should you buy?

sections.title: Choosing an agent: buy the right amount of autonomy

blocks.body: Autonomy is not a trophy. It is a setting. A human should not hand over a task simply because an agent can attempt it, just as a team should not manually repeat a safe, well-specified check that a machine can perform reliably. The useful choice depends on uncertainty, consequence, reversibility and the quality of available evidence.

blocks.title: Use a risk-adjusted decision
blocks.body:
Reading a CI log and drafting an explanation has a different risk from merging the proposed fix. The investigation can often run unattended while the merge still requires a reviewer. Autonomy does not have to be granted to the whole workflow at once.

Ask where an error would be noticed and how it would be undone. A patch on an isolated branch is relatively easy to inspect and discard. A public message, data migration or production change may be harder to reverse even when the command itself is simple.

Put review at the transition where it can change the outcome. Approval after an irreversible action is only an audit. If the objective itself is disputed or the evidence cannot support a decision, bring a person in before implementation begins.

blocks.bridge: The best agent is the one whose level of autonomy matches the task, not the one with the most impressive demo.
blocks.meaning: Risk, uncertainty and reversibility determine how much delegation is sensible.
blocks.question: Which task is the better first candidate for autonomy: formatting a known set of files or deleting production data?
blocks.answer: Formatting the known files. It is bounded, observable and reversible; production deletion demands a much stronger approval boundary.

further.question: Why does reversibility matter?
further.answer: It reduces the cost of a wrong action and makes experimentation safer.

further.question: When is a human the right choice?
further.answer: When the objective or evidence requires judgment that cannot be made legible enough for safe delegation, especially before irreversible consequences.

blocks.title: A team wants an agent to own a dependency upgrade.
blocks.problem: A team wants an agent to own a dependency upgrade.

steps.title: Start at a safe boundary
steps.body: Let it inspect the dependency, propose the version change, run the focused tests and produce a diff.
steps.reason: The team gets useful work with a clear review point.
steps.trap: Allowing an automatic publish on the first trial.

steps.title: Expand by evidence
steps.body: After repeated successful trials, consider automatic branch creation or merge checks, while keeping release changes gated.
steps.trap: Treating a high benchmark score as permission for production actions.

blocks.title: Prefer a smaller promise you can prove
blocks.body: A modest agent that produces a reviewable patch may beat a powerful agent that takes broad action with opaque evidence. Start with the narrowest autonomy that could deliver value, measure the result and expand only when the failure modes are understood.

blocks.bridge: Autonomy should expand from evidence, not optimism.
blocks.meaning: Start with a narrow promise, measure the outcome and use what you learn to set the next boundary.
blocks.question: What should a team measure before increasing autonomy?
blocks.answer: Task success, defect escape, review effort, recovery time, cost and the quality of evidence accompanying decisions.

further.question: Why include review effort?
further.answer: A result that takes longer to verify than to produce may not be an efficiency gain.

further.question: What is a good expansion rule?
further.answer: Increase scope only when the existing scope has reliable checks and known recovery paths.

data.title: Lab 5 · Choose an autonomy boundary
data.brief: Take one real engineering task and decide which actions an agent may inspect, propose, apply and publish.
steps: Describe the task's uncertainty, consequence, reversibility and available checks.
Draw four boundaries: read, propose, apply and publish.
Run a narrow trial and record success, review effort, recovery and escaped defects.
Use the evidence to keep, narrow or expand one boundary.
deliverables: A trial report with an expansion decision
data.review: A good decision explains why each boundary matches the task's risk and names the evidence that would justify changing it. 'The agent seemed capable' is not enough.

blocks.body: Buy the amount of autonomy you can supervise, verify and recover from; expand only when evidence earns it.

data.governingLaw: Long-horizon work requires explicit state, checkpoints, bounded progress, and recovery rather than one uninterrupted context. The right autonomy level is the least powerful arrangement that can meet the task's evidence and risk requirements.
data.invariant: A resumed run must re-establish task identity and evidence before continuing from a checkpoint. Escalation changes authority only when the acceptance test and rollback path remain explicit.
data.limitingCase: For a one-step task, checkpointing costs more than it saves and adds no recovery value. When the task is ambiguous or irreversible, supervised assistance can be the maximum justified autonomy.
data.counterexample: More turns do not imply more progress when the agent repeats an action without changing its hypothesis. Automating a frequent task can reduce throughput if review, recovery, and maintenance cost exceed the saved effort.
data.validity: Long-horizon reliability depends on recoverable state and measurable progress, not on context length alone. An autonomy choice is valid only for the named task, environment, risk tolerance, and evidence contract.
